title: SQLAlchemy Models & Relationships
description: Define database models and relationships (one-to-many, many-to-many) using SQLAlchemy ORM.
content:
Hello! Welcome back to our module on Database Modeling with SQLAlchemy. In the last lesson, we designed the conceptual blueprint for our application's data—a normalized relational database schema. You learned how to structure tables and define relationships to ensure data integrity and prevent common anomalies. This is the "what" and "why" of our data architecture. Today, we bridge the gap between that abstract design and our Python application. This lesson addresses the learning outcome: **Define database models and relationships (one-to-many, many-to-many) using SQLAlchemy ORM.** You will learn how to translate your SQL schema into Python classes that our FastAPI application can work with directly. This is a fundamental skill for building clean, maintainable, and type-safe backend systems. ### 1. From SQL Tables to Python Classes: The Role of an ORM An Object-Relational Mapper (ORM) is a library that automates the transfer of data between a relational database (like PostgreSQL) and an object-oriented programming language (like Python). Instead of writing raw SQL queries as strings, you interact with Python objects and methods. Coming from PyMongo, you're familiar with the concept of an Object-Document Mapper (ODM), where you map Python objects to MongoDB documents. The principle of an ORM is similar: you manipulate Python objects. The key difference is that the ORM maps these objects to the structured, relational tables and relationships you designed in the previous lesson, enforcing the schema at the application level. ### 2. Defining a Basic Model with SQLAlchemy 2.0 Let's start by defining a simple table as a Python class. We will use the modern, fully type-annotated style introduced in SQLAlchemy 2.0. This is the current best practice and what you'll encounter in modern codebases. ```grasp { "type": "reading", "title": "A little SQLAlchemy 2.0 guide", "id": "[LINK](https://medium.com/@artur.rakhmatulin/a-little-sqlalchemy-2-0-guide-66090ea2b3f9)", "url": "https://medium.com/@artur.rakhmatulin/a-little-sqlalchemy-2-0-guide-66090ea2b3f9", "relevant_section_indices": [ 0 ], "par_intro": "To understand the modern syntax, let's start with a guide that clearly contrasts the old and new ways of defining models and explains the benefits of the new approach.", "par_directions": "Read the section 'A little about Models definition'. Focus on understanding the new syntax using `Mapped` and `mapped_column`. Pay attention to the rule: Python types go in `Mapped[]`, and SQLAlchemy/SQL types go in `mapped_column()`.", "estimated_time": "10 minutes" } ``` Let's break down the core components from that reading: 1. **`DeclarativeBase`**: All of your models will inherit from a central base class. This base class holds a registry of all models, which is how SQLAlchemy knows which tables exist in your schema. 2. **`__tablename__`**: This special attribute tells SQLAlchemy the name of the database table to which this class should be mapped. 3. **`Mapped` and `mapped_column`**: This is the modern syntax for defining a column. * `Mapped[]`: This is a type annotation. It tells your IDE and static analysis tools (like Mypy) what Python type to expect for this attribute (e.g., `int`, `str`, `datetime`). * `mapped_column(, ...)`: This function call defines the actual database column, its type (e.g., `Integer`, `String`), and its constraints (e.g., `primary_key=True`, `unique=True`). Here's how we'd define a simple `User` model, translating the concepts from our last lesson into code: ```python from sqlalchemy import Integer, String from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column # 1. Define the base class for all models class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass # 2. Define a model for the 'users' table class User(Base): __tablename__ = "users" # Define columns using the modern, typed syntax id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(Integer, primary_key=True) username: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(50), unique=True, nullable=False) email: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(100), unique=True, nullable=False) def __repr__(self): return f"" ``` This code is clean, readable, and provides excellent autocompletion and error-checking in modern editors, which is a significant advantage in large projects. ### 3. Defining Relationships: One-to-Many Relationships are what make a relational database powerful. Let's model a **one-to-many** relationship. Recall our blog example: a `User` can have many `Posts`, but each `Post` is written by exactly one `User`. In SQLAlchemy, this is achieved using two components: 1. **`ForeignKey`**: This is placed inside a `mapped_column` on the "many" side of the relationship (`Post`). Since you're comfortable with SQL, you can think of this as the Python equivalent of the `FOREIGN KEY (...) REFERENCES ...` constraint in your `CREATE TABLE` statement. 2. **`relationship()`**: This is a higher-level ORM construct. It creates a "magic" attribute on your model that allows you to navigate between the related Python objects (e.g., access a list of posts via `some_user.posts`). It doesn't create a real column in the database. Here is the complete example: ```python from typing import List from sqlalchemy import Integer, String, ForeignKey from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, relationship class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass class User(Base): __tablename__ = "users" id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True) username: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(50), unique=True, nullable=False) # This relationship creates the `user.posts` attribute posts: Mapped[List["Post"]] = relationship(back_populates="author") class Post(Base): __tablename__ = "posts" id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True) title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(100), nullable=False) # This column holds the foreign key to the 'users' table author_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("users.id")) # This relationship creates the `post.author` attribute # and links it back to the `User.posts` relationship author: Mapped["User"] = relationship(back_populates="posts") ``` The `back_populates` argument is crucial for a **bidirectional** relationship. It tells SQLAlchemy that `User.posts` and `Post.author` refer to the two sides of the same relationship. When you append a new `Post` to a `User`'s `posts` list, SQLAlchemy will automatically set the `author` attribute on that `Post` object for you, keeping everything in sync. ### 4. Defining Relationships: Many-to-Many Many-to-many relationships require an intermediary table, often called an **association table** or **join table**. For example, a `Student` can enroll in many `Courses`, and a `Course` can have many `Students`. ```grasp { "type": "image", "title": "Many-to-Many Relationship Example in a Relational Database", "id": "[LINK](https://datasciencepartners.nl/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/sql-many-to-many-relationship-voorbeeld.png)", "url": "https://datasciencepartners.nl/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/sql-many-to-many-relationship-voorbeeld.png", "caption": "This diagram shows the classic structure for a many-to-many relationship. The `course_subscriptions` table links `students` and `courses`. Each row in `course_subscriptions` represents one student enrolling in one course." } ``` To implement this in SQLAlchemy, you need three things: 1. The two primary models (`Student`, `Course`). 2. An **association table** object that defines the intermediary table (`course_subscriptions`). 3. A `relationship()` on both primary models that uses the `secondary` argument to point to the association table. The following resource provides a clear, production-grade example of defining complex many-to-many relationships. ```grasp { "type": "reading", "title": "Building a Modern User Permission Management System ...", "id": "[LINK](https://dev.to/mochafreddo/building-a-modern-user-permission-management-system-with-fastapi-sqlalchemy-and-mariadb-5fp1)", "url": "https://dev.to/mochafreddo/building-a-modern-user-permission-management-system-with-fastapi-sqlalchemy-and-mariadb-5fp1", "relevant_section_indices": [ 1 ], "par_intro": "Let's examine a complete example of modeling many-to-many relationships for a user permission system. This will show you how to define the association tables and link them to your primary models.", "par_directions": "In the section 'Database Models with SQLAlchemy 2.0', focus on how the `user_roles` association table is defined using `sqlalchemy.Table`. Then, look at the `User` and `Role` models to see how `relationship(secondary=user_roles, ...)` is used to link them together.", "estimated_time": "15 minutes" } ``` Let's adapt that pattern to our `Student` and `Course` example. First, we define the association table. Notice that it's just a `Table` object, not a full model class, because it doesn't contain any extra information beyond the foreign keys. ```python from sqlalchemy import Table, Column, Integer, ForeignKey # ... (Base class definition) ... # Define the association table student_course_association = Table( "student_course_association", Base.metadata, Column("student_id", Integer, ForeignKey("students.id"), primary_key=True), Column("course_id", Integer, ForeignKey("courses.id"), primary_key=True), ) ``` Now, we define our primary models and use `secondary` to link them via this table. ```python # ... (imports and Base class) ... class Student(Base): __tablename__ = "students" id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True) name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(100), nullable=False) # The M-M relationship to Course courses: Mapped[List["Course"]] = relationship( secondary=student_course_association, back_populates="students" ) class Course(Base): __tablename__ = "courses" id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True) title: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(100), nullable=False) # The M-M relationship back to Student students: Mapped[List["Student"]] = relationship( secondary=student_course_association, back_populates="courses" ) ``` With this setup, you can now do things like `some_student.courses.append(some_course)`, and SQLAlchemy will automatically create the corresponding row in the `student_course_association` table when you commit your changes.
Test your understanding! You need to model a system for tagging articles. An `Article` can have multiple `Tags`, and a `Tag` can be applied to multiple `Articles`. 1. How many models and/or tables do you need to define? What would you name them? 2. On the `Article` model, how would you define the relationship to `Tag`? What are the key arguments to `relationship()`?
Show answer 1. You need three database objects in total: * An `Article` model class. * A `Tag` model class. * An association table, which we could call `article_tags_association`. 2. On the `Article` model, you would define the relationship like this: ```python class Article(Base): __tablename__ = "articles" # ... id, title, etc. tags: Mapped[List["Tag"]] = relationship( secondary=article_tags_association, back_populates="articles" ) ``` The key arguments are `secondary`, which points to the association table object, and `back_populates`, which links it to the corresponding relationship on the `Tag` model (`Tag.articles`).
### Conclusion You have now learned how to translate a conceptual database schema into concrete, type-safe Python code using SQLAlchemy ORM. This is a critical step in building a robust backend, as it allows your application logic to interact with the database in a safe and intuitive way. **Key Takeaways:** * **Models are Python Classes:** In SQLAlchemy, database tables are represented by Python classes that inherit from a `DeclarativeBase`. * **Modern Syntax is Typed:** Use `Mapped` and `mapped_column` to define columns with clear Python type hints, improving code quality and developer experience. * **One-to-Many Relationships** are defined using a `ForeignKey` on the "many" side and a `relationship()` on both sides (linked with `back_populates`). * **Many-to-Many Relationships** require a third, intermediary **association table** and are defined using the `secondary` argument in the `relationship()` function. **Next Up:** We've defined our models, but they exist only in our Python code. The next step is to make our application aware of an actual database. In the next lesson, you will learn how to **connect a FastAPI application to a PostgreSQL database using SQLAlchemy**, setting up the engine and session management required to start persisting data.
